newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Oil firms crowding into growing Indochina market.
newsitem.headline: Oil firms crowding into growing Indochina market.

text.p: Indochina's fledgling oil markets are attracting many foreign suppliers and traders seeking a piece of the action in anticipation of booming economies and rising demand, industry sources say.

"Indochina does have potential," said a trader with an oil major, referring to Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. "It is the last bastion in the region's growing economies while the rest are getting saturated."
But industry players are concerned Indochina could become overcrowded if demand fails to keep pace with the number of companies operating in the region or exporting products there.
Other concerns are the political instability in Cambodia, despite its open market system, and Vietnam's closed market.

Among companies with varying degrees of operations in Cambodia are French Total SA, Caltex, a joint-venture between U.S. Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc, Malaysia's Petronas, Royal/Dutch Shell and Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT).

Marubeni International Petroleum Corp (Mipco), a unit of Japan's Marubeni Corp, is positioning itself in Cambodia. It is in a joint venture with Cambodia's independent oil firm Sokimex to upgrade an oil product storage in the southern deep-sea port of Sihanoukville to 50,000 barrels per day (bpd) from 30,000 bpd, a Mipco source said.
The project, which will include upgrading an oil jetty, is due for completion by fourth quarter 1997.

Cambodia's diesel and gasoline imports are 600,000-700,000 tonnes a year, the source said. Oil demand is growing at 10 percent a year, amid projected annual gross domestic product growth of 7.5 percent until 2000.
Sokimex has 60-70 percent of Cambodia's market. Mipco plans to supply half its stocks through the new terminal, he said.

Mipco is trying to invest in Laos, but the market is small and relies mostly on hydropower which limits its potential for oil sales, sources said. Annual diesel and gasoline demand is 300,000 tonnes and growth rate just five percent.

A Total source in Phnom Penh said the company has an 8,000-cubic-meter storage depot in the country, equally divided between diesel and gasoline. The depot supplies Total's marketing network of 20 stations and is targeting 10 more in the next two years, he said.
Traders said firms like Mipco have to compete with Thailand's PTT and Vietnam's state-owned trader Petrolimex who are already entrenched in Cambodia.

PTT views Laos, Cambodia, Burma and southern China as its niche market area because of its proximity and cultural affinity, said a PTT source. PTT is working on building a storage depot in Cambodia where it has three service stations.

"Demand in Cambodia is concentrated in Phnom Penh, as it is still dangerous to supply the rest of the country because of booby traps," the PTT source said. "But if you don't establish your market first, how can you raise your market share?"
PTT is venturing into Burma despite political uncertainties there, he said.

Traders said Vietnam has closed its retail market to foreign firms, but almost all of its oil products demand is met by imports, which are then sold under regulated conditions. Vietnam is expected to import 2.5 million tonnes of diesel in 1996 with an annual demand growth of 12-15 percent.

Traders said many suppliers are ready to sell aggressively into Vietnam, such as Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC), which has a one-year diesel contract and Mipco, which has a nine-month deal. Spot suppliers include Singapore trader Hin Leong, Japan's Sumitomo Trading, South Korea's Yukong Ltd, Shell and Esso, a unit of Exxon Corp.
